speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FIFTEENTH ANNIVERSARY OF ENTRANCE OF NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before we proceed I think the house will agree, particularly in view of the fact that the provinces are foregathered in Quebec, that today it would be appropriate in this house to mark the fifteenth anniversary of the entry of Newfoundland into confederation. I am sure our association with that province in the Canadian family will mark a period of national unity in which citizens in all parts of Canada will share in the prestige and achievements of our country.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: FIFTEENTH ANNIVERSARY OF ENTRANCE OF NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will agree with the sentiments expressed by the Acting Prime Minister. The entry of Newfoundland into confederation brought about the achievement of a dream which existed from the days prior to confederation and throughout the intervening years, and made possible the establishment of one Canada. Indeed, as one enters the House of Commons and sees those words "The wholesome sea is at her gates, her gates both east and west," one must conclude the writer forgot her gates to the north, but all those seas actually became part of our country on the entry of Newfoundland into confederation, to which it has given so notable a contribution.

subtopic: FIFTEENTH ANNIVERSARY OF ENTRANCE OF NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of the New Democratic party would like to associate themselves with the remarks which have been made by the Acting Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in commemorating the fifteenth anniversary of Newfoundland's entrance into Canadian confederation.
I think all of us believe that Newfoundland joining the Canadian family has been a good thing for Newfoundland and for Canada. We trust this newest member of the Canadian family will long enjoy its association, that the spirit of unity which brought Newfoundland into confederation will permeate all the provinces of Canada and that we shall continue to build in the spirit of unity, a great nation on this northern half of the North American continent.

subtopic: FIFTEENTH ANNIVERSARY OF ENTRANCE OF NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the Social Credit party join with the Acting Prime Minister and the leaders of the other opposition parties in expressing our own feeling of gratitude on this fifteenth anniversary of Newfoundland's entry into confederation, at the progress that has been made, and at the general attitude of Canadianism that has been displayed by these our youngest brethren.
I think there is a lesson to be learned from Newfoundland, a lesson that has been developing during the last fifteen years in which the people of Newfoundland have become thoroughly convinced of the benefits which are theirs in being part of Canada. You may recall, sir, that when the decision was made to come into Canada it was only a very small majority of the people of Newfoundland who thought that was the right thing to do, but today there is practically a unanimous feeling amongst those people, and they are happy and proud to be part of Canada. This is a lesson which we should be more conscious of than we are.

subtopic: FIFTEENTH ANNIVERSARY OF ENTRANCE OF NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when Newfoundland joined the great Canadian family, 15 years ago, I was a member of this house and we welcomed Newfoundland into our confederation with enthusiasm.
Since then the people of Newfoundland have sometimes wondered whether they had taken a good step forward and done the right thing in becoming part of Canada. Today I think Newfoundland is perfectly happy to be one of the Canadian provinces.
On this anniversary I wish Newfoundlanders a great deal of prosperity and an ever-increasing contribution to the emancipation of each of the Canadian provinces. We are very glad to extend to that province our wishes for many more years within the Canadian confederation.

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext: I believe the minister of northern affairs has been designated as the minister to give attention to the plight of those who have been adversely affected by the flood in the Alberni valley. I should like to ask the hon. gentleman if he could give the house any report as to what the government have done to help the victims of this disaster, and what plans they have to assist those who are in need.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext:
I think yesterday the deputy provincial secretary in Victoria, Mr. Lawrence Wallace, asked for the intervention of the army, and within a very few hours there was a reconnaissance party in Alberni. Beginning, I think, at midnight last night the army started moving in a total of 240 men, and today at noon they began bringing in some heavy equipment designed, I believe, to repair municipal services in the general area.
I want to tell the hon. member that, thankfully, it would now appear that the over-all damage is much less than was at first anticipated. This does not in any way detract from the enormous loss to individuals. We are now informed, on a preliminary basis, that 45 houses have been totally destroyed, some 14 have been very severely damaged, and 375 more houses have more or less damage. This, of course, is a very severe loss, and is one reason why this morning I sent a wire to Hon. Wesley Black, minister of social welfare, asking him to supply us with a copy of the assessment of the damage to these private properties and to give us some indication of how they intended to compensate these people who otherwise are not covered by insurance at all. This is the nature of the severity in that area and, of course, to these individual persons it is extremely severe.
I understand that inquiries are being made concerning a disaster fund that I think still exists in the province of British Columbia.
Inquiries of the Ministry It is in charge of one or two trustees, and that fund may be released. In addition, a new disaster fund has been started. I think the hon. member himself is probably the only member present in the house who visited the scene last Saturday. He gave his commendation to that fund, and I understand that very worth-while contributions are being made. I think we should all assist this fund, because it is an excellent exercise in humanism in itself.
I was talking to Mayor Fred Bishop of Alberni this morning, and he advised me that the civic leaders there, and indeed the people, were most gratified at the action taken by all levels of government and by the various agencies that are contributing to overcome the difficulty in the area.

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the fact that the most pressing need is for assistance to the people who have been rendered homeless-I understand there are 77 families with no roof over their heads and another 233 families who have been placed with their neighbours, and that these people need bedding, clothing, cooking utensils, dishes and furniture so they can be taken care of-has the government given any consideration to the possibility of making a substantial contribution to the Alberni valley disaster fund, which might be the most immediate way of helping those who are in need at the present time, pending looking into the question of rehabilitation?

Mr. Chairman, when the house rose last evening I was dealing with a question from the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) in connection with butter exports. He had referred to the fact that the United Kingdom had made some increases in its butter import quota this year, and he wanted to know whether we would be participating in that trade.
The situation is that in April, 1962 when the United Kingdom butter market was seriously depressed under very heavy imports, the government of that country placed butter imports under quota and gave quotas to the regular supplying countries. Canada is not a regular commercial supplier of butter to the United Kingdom, and indeed the price of butter in this country does not permit Canadian exporters to engage in competitive world trade at world prices.
However, last fall when there was a temporary shortage of butter in the United Kingdom the government of that country issued a special open quota, and Canada was able to participate in this to the extent of some 5] million pounds, at of course considerably subsidized prices. There has, as the hon. member stated, been a minor increase in United Kingdom quotas this year to regular suppliers. If these countries are not able to meet their quotas, or if a shortage should develop in the United Kingdom, we would hope that Canada would again be able to participate in some business, as we did last fall.
In addition to butter, we have been able to dispose of some 18 million pounds of butter oil, including 4J million pounds to the United Kingdom. I can only add that we are actively endeavouring to secure additional outlets for the heavy accumulation of butter since 1957, and there are some encouraging prospects that more trade will develop.

The hon. member for Kent commented on the support program for two crops in which his area specializes, namely soybeans and sugar beets. The support program for the forthcoming year for both of these commodities is under study by the agricultural stabilization board and it is expected that their recommendations will be made shortly. In the meantime it should be pointed out that the current support price for soybeans is the highest that has ever been in effect and is set at 100 per cent of the base price.
While sugar beets produced during 1963 were supported at the highest percentage ever in effect, namely 109 per cent of the base price, it is not anticipated that returns to producers will fall to the support level. I am sure that hon. members will be interested to know that in Ontario the growers last year received an average of $15.58 per ton for their sugar beets, all of which was paid to them by the processors, compared with a total of $11.58 in the previous year, of which $3.08 consisted of government payments, both federal and provincial. In this connection it should be noted that the payments received in any one year refer to the return on beets harvested in the fall of the previous year.

I might say in this connection that I am sure some of our government reports are a

The hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska referred to hide prices and requested the reason for the difference between the prices quoted for hides by the dominion bureau of statistics and the prices received by farmers in his area. I regret that I have not yet been able to get information to clarify this matter entirely. I will however have the inquiry pursued. In the meantime I am informed that the dominion bureau of statistics quoted price is based on what are called salted hides, which are hides that have gone through certain stages of preparation prior to tanning and are of a certain standard of quality. While without further information it is impossible to account completely for the differences quoted by the hon. member, it is entirely possible that differences in quality, methods of preparation and distance from markets may account for much of the price difference.

just a moment. It seems to me that someone asked about policy in so far as agriculture is concerned. I should like to assure hon. members that any policies that are good for the farmer will not be torn down. We are going to improve them if it is at all possible.
Shortly after the war, in 1946, I met a group of agriculturists in the city of Buenos Aires. They asked me, what do you think Argentina is famous for? I think probably every person in the world would have no problem in saying Argentina is famous for the production of beef. I asked them, in turn, if Argentina is famous for the production of beef, for what is Canada famous? They said paper and pulp, wheat and dairy cattle. This rather impressed me because you can ask the same question of anyone today in about 30 countries and you will receive the same answer.
It seems to me that any agricultural policy we formulate should have due regard for our geographical position. We have 482,000 farmers in Canada who are vigorous, who have a lot of get up and go. I think they could be producing a good many lines of seed stock that are required around the world, not only for livestock but for grains and vegetables. I believe this is the sort of thing that should be considered in any policy we establish. What has happened to our hog production in Canada in the last seven to ten years? We know the job that the Danes have done with their hog

Supply-Agriculture
production and their famous bacon. We know that with the same amount of feed they have a return of $4 more per hog, and when you multiply this by approximately 140,000 hogs produced in Canada each week and then multiply that by the number for the year you will realize that our farmers are losing between $30 million and $40 million a year.
I could go on to deal with other products. I believe that we, in Canada, have a job to do in so far as efficiency is concerned. We should remember that a yield of two more bushels per acre gives our farmers $100 million more. In so far as swine are concerned we have a job to do, the same as we have done in connection with dairy cattle, which are in demand all over the world. I believe that it should be our policy to harness these 56 experimental stations we have in the research department that are doing an excellent job. We should also harness all these exhibitions, so that we can tie up every group and perhaps direct them into producing seed stock for the rest of the world. I look forward to the year 1964. We know that 1963 was a record year for agriculture, and we face 1964 with hope. We know that climatic conditions may change the results for any year, but we are looking forward to having the biggest year we have ever had in 1964.

There was one question which I thought perhaps I might answer because I think it was more properly directed to the statement I made the other day than to the statement made by my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture. Perhaps I might dispose of that particular question if the hon. member for Provencher would not mind.
Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition said, as will be found in Hansard at page 1572:
-as yet we have had no information as to what actually took place during those 17 days.
This was from February 3 to February 20.
In particular, we want to be furnished with a record of all the directives and orders made by the Minister of Agriculture between those two dates in connection with the branches which were transferred to the Minister of Forestry.
The right hon. gentleman, on Thursday, as recorded on page 1520 of Hansard, made a reference to this matter in these terms:
I think they will have to pass an order in council to ratify what was done.
This was at the very conclusion of what he had to say.
Indeed, when they have done that they will have to come before the house and ask, and they will receive-ask and ye shall receive-forgiveness for what they did and legalization for what they ought not to have done.
Now, sir, I did in the observations I made last Thursday give all the information that

the officials had been able to gather for me or that I had been able to gather for myself on this particular point. Up to that time research had indicated that the only thing the minister had done personally, in his personal capacity in respect of those things under the order of February 3 that had been transferred to the Minister of Forestry, was to sign those eight ARDA agreements. Of course, the officials had proceeded under the authority given to them by the minister to do the things that are normally done in the department. I indicated also that happens in every case of the transfer of duties. It also happens in every case of the transfer of ministers. I have a good many examples I could give. I do not believe anyone has ever maintained there is anything illegal about that. Government would be paralysed if the authority given by one minister was not valid until a new authority had been signed by another minister. I think everyone with any experience in government knows that.
That is quite different from the situation here.

In the case of the transfer of duties of the travel bureau, which I think was the last case under the government of the right hon. gentleman, 77 days elapsed between the passing of the order and the completion of all these authorizations. There
is,	therefore, nothing unusual in these matters at all.
However I believe the government owes a most complete explanation to the house about this matter. I have no hesitation in saying that the government is responsible to the House of Commons. I have always maintained this doctrine from both sides of the house, and have done my utmost to uphold
it.	I am going, right here and now, to ask my colleague the Minister of Justice if he will have the officers of his department look at the whole record of this period very carefully. It will not be completed within a day or two, but I doubt if it will take very long. I am going to ask him if he will have them do this with the utmost diligence. If the house will allow us, we would then do what the right hon. gentleman has said, and that, is if anything needs to be rectified, we would do our best to rectify it. We would come here frankly and explain what had been done. I hope the minister will feel that he is able to give the undertaking I have suggested.

The observations made by the Minister of Transport are of such a nature that naturally the house will accept his undertaking to do what I believe should have been done earlier. However, that is all past now. I would point out that the suggestion that what has taken place here had any

relationship whatever to the transfer of duties for the tourist bureau is a preposterous statement. In this case there was an entire vesting of the powers over a particular department, or sectors of a department, on February 3. Was there anything done by the Minister of Agriculture during that period of time, until February 20, which would not be legal? If the Minister of Justice will have this looked into in the manner suggested by the Minister of Transport and a report given to the house, that will clarify the situation.
Then there should be legalization of whatever is found to require further action in order to ratify and approve what has been done. I am sure, in the spirit in which the minister has placed the matter before the committee, namely that if wrong has been done and serious error committed the government will ask for forgiveness, then in the spirit not only of Easter, to which reference was made today, but as always in the spirit of this house, we will do our part to assure that what ought not to have been done and was done will be corrected.

Mr. Chairman, we witnessed today one of those very rare occasions when the Minister of Transport comes before us in sack cloth and ashes and seeks repentance for those things he ought not to have done. The confession made by the minister will considerably shorten my remarks this afternoon, as I was going to make the plea that he give consideration to the government's reviewing of the events of those fateful 17 days and to introducing a remedial measure to take care of the mistakes and errors committed during that period.
We on this side are very pleased to see the Minister of Agriculture in his place today and to hear him make a statement that covered a wide range of subjects. I do not intend to go over all those subjects, but we on this side would like to discuss agricultural policy a little more fully with him, and particularly to discuss those aspects of the department which have a bearing on what can be done to relieve pockets of distress in agriculture, the low income farmers in distressed areas, and those parts of agriculture which are not enjoying the degree of prosperity that agriculture in general is enjoying.
Supply-Agriculture
Despite all the statistics quoted to show the agricultural situation is improving, there are always pockets of distress, and most of the branches of the minister's department which could have been helpful in those areas are now transferred out of his jurisdiction. Last night he suggested he still had some 30 odd branches to take care of. He gave the impression that he was tremendously overworked, and that it was going to be difficult for him to keep track of all the problems he would be faced with in administering the branches that remain under his jurisdiction.
He certainly did not take that attitude when he first assumed the portfolio. He was running about the country auctioning bulls all over the place, and never seemed to worry whether the Department of Agriculture had any administrative leadership. But now when he has lost part of his department he suggests there is too much for him to do, and that therefore he was quite agreeable to the transfer of some of his responsibilities.
During the course of this and the preceding session of parliament we have posed a good many questions to the government and have received a variety of answers, but I am beginning to wonder how much we can depend upon the word of ministers when they reply to questions asked by members of the opposition. As recorded at page 3632 of Hansard for October 16, 1963 the hon. member for Kootenay West wanted to know where the Minister of Agriculture was on the previous day, when there was a debate in the house on agricultural matters. The Prime Minister replied that the minister and his associate at that time were away in the west, looking after the grass roots, but it turned out that the minister was in Kingston selling bulls. I wonder, are we going to have a continuation of this type of misleading statements and answers to our questions.
Again, as recorded at page 2608 of Hansard for July 25, 1963, the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle asked the minister whether he could report to the house on the resignation of his acting assistant deputy minister, Dr. Krist-jansson, and in reply the minister said:
Mr. Speaker, I know of no intention on the part of anyone to resign. Everyone seems very, very happy.
I ask, why did Dr. Kristjansson leave the department? I think the answer was given the other day by the hon. member for Port Arthur when he referred to the events taking place within the department in regard to ARDA. Dr. Kristjansson was one of those men who pushed the ARDA program, who believed in it and what it could do. The fact that he left the department is an indication that the

Supply-A griculture
minister cared little what transpired, or what direction was given to the department in regard to ARDA.
I have just been advised, and I wish to put this on the record, also, that Dr. Krist-jansson had resigned the day before the question was asked, and the minister did not know anything about it. This gives some indication of how much he knows about what is going on within his department.
Just the other day the hon. member for Skeena asked a question regarding cold storage, to which the minister replied that he had been taking a very close look at the problem. This is something the minister is doing all the time. He is the closest looking person I have ever known. No matter what question is asked, he says he is going to take a close look at it. Members of the government have been examining problems minutely for the past year, but we have not seen any results of this examination.
The minister said, as recorded at page 1525 of Hansard for March 26:
In so far as cold storage is concerned, we have taken a very close look at every application we have received and most of them have been approved. Hon. members will remember that the previous government had an austerity program and cold storage grants were frozen.
A little later the hon. member referred back to this particular point and said:
I wonder whether I could pose one question to the minister about cold storage activities. I think the minister said that in the last few weeks they have approved more applications under the Cold Storage Act than were approved in the previous 18 months.
The minister replied:
This figure may not be too accurate-
I wholly agree with that statement. The figures and information given to us on many matters concerning agriculture are certainly not too accurate.
On the same day the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska posed a question to the minister concerning hides, and the minister replied:
I do not know. I cannot answer this question, and I am sure no one else can answer it. The law of supply and demand enters into these
things__ This is the first time I have heard of
it.
Well, he left the impression that this was news to him. Then on Monday, in his statement, he refers to the same subject again and says: "As a matter of fact, several people who have thousands of hides in store have come to see me and they have been to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce". So this was not such a new matter, after all, two days later. So, on the strength of these statements which have been made in the house constantly by members of the government I do

not think members of this house will wonder at all why we are constantly putting questions to this government in an effort to get answers in which we can place some faith.
I have dealt with the question of misleading statements. The minister said last night that he was overworked. I wonder just how much work there is left for him to do when most of his department has disappeared from under him. What has he got left? Is there such a great effort involved in the administration of the act concerning race track betting? I wonder how many hours a day he spends on that. He must be overworked providing leadership in connection with the pest control act. Perhaps he could broaden its scope a little so as to include some of his colleagues in the cabinet, and bring them under control. I am sure great qualities of leadership are needed to take care of the administration under the Live Stock Pedigree Act. I give the minister credit for putting up a valiant struggle to retain some portion of his department.
We all know that some of these duties are administrative in nature but there are several important facets to the department, branches which will play a very important part in the development of agriculture. The farm credit program is one of them; PFRA is another. The price stabilization board and the crop insurance program are also important parts of the department which require leadership and administration. I hope the minister will be left to provide this administration. I should like to believe him when he says he has the interest of the farmers at heart and that he is anxious to pursue policies which are beneficial to agriculture. I think perhaps he will do that, if he is left alone to do it. But I am a little suspicious about that group which was there in 1957 and prior to that time-that bunch which ignored and completely forgot the western farmers, and farmers in general in this country, and we are a little concerned that the minister may be pressured from all sides to do little and to do less. I can assure him he has the wholehearted support of members on this side of the house, if he has any battles to fight with other members of the cabinet.
The minister told us there was to be a liaison committee consisting of three members, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Forestry. After reading some of the statements which have been made by those ministers I am seriously in doubt as to what type of co-operation one can expect from three men who have such varied views on matters having to do with agriculture. The Minister of Forestry takes one view, the Minister of Agriculture takes another and

the Minister of Trade and Commerce, whose statements we have heard much about in western Canada, seems to hold a third view. We sincerely hope there will be some co-ordination of effort between these three ministers, because having regard to the way in which responsibilities have been taken away from the Minister of Agriculture, the closest co-operation will certainly be required if there is to be any co-ordination of agricultural policy. We certainly hope to see evidence that this troika, as someone has called it, can work and produce effective legislation.
The minister takes great pleasure these days in referring to the progress made by agriculture when he visits the constituencies. I think he can do this with some justifiable pride because the income from agriculture is improving. But I challenge him to give us one instance of any action taken either by the government or by himself which has resulted in the improvement of the agricultural situation in this country, other than the continuation of those policies which were instituted by the previous government.
In conclusion, let me say this: We should like to assist the minister in every way possible. We should like to make sure that he appears before the house occasionally to give us a review of his activities. We are looking forward to the debate on the estimates of his department during which we can discuss policy in general. I should include, at this point, a reference to the Minister of Forestry who now holds an important portfolio-the administration of the ARDA program and its related branches. This is a most important program as far as agriculture is concerned. We should like to know what the government's proposals are, what its hopes are and what its plans are. We hope there will be co-ordination, though I am sometimes doubtful how those hopes will materialize.
I have here a copy of an article which appeared in Time magazine last fall. This is required reading. Discussing the new Liberal government, it says:
The new Pearson government is, by common consent, better staffed with cabinet talent-
We look across the floor and wonder where the writer of this article got that idea.
-and has a clearer view of the direction it intends to take-
"All directions" is about the answer to that.
-than any previous incoming Canadian administration. It has thought out its position on defence-
We have had some examples of how clearly they thought out that position. The article goes on:
Supply-Agriculture
-on foreign affairs, on biculturalism, and it has done its homework in economics.
We shall ask the Minister of Finance about that. I prefer to say that as far as I am concerned this government, like Christopher Columbus, did not know where they were going, did not know where they were when they got there, did not know where they had been when they got back, and they did it on borrowed money.

Mr. Chairman, we are now discussing supplementary estimates for the Department of Agriculture amounting to $127,343,681, and this amount raises the estimates of this department for the fiscal year ending March 31 to $300,564,831. These figures leave us thoughtful, considering the minor importance given by the government to Canadian agriculture, especially to the farmers of eastern Canada.
The main estimates for 1962-63 merely allotted $161 million to agriculture, while in the main estimates for 1963-64, the amount was $172 million.
We are now being asked to approve supplementary estimates in the amount of $127 million, thus raising the total to more than $300 million. However, if we consider the 1963-64 estimates, we find that the total estimated expenditures are of $140,124,860. It is therefore obvious that we shall be asked again during the next session to pass another series of supplementary estimates.
On the other hand, if we consider the total estimated expenditures in the main estimates, we find that in 1963-64, agriculture accounted for only 2.7 per cent of the expenditures and that for 1964-65, it accounts for only 2.1 per cent, or a decrease of .6 per cent.
Who will support this decrease which comes at a time when expenditures are increasing? Certainly not the western farmers who had the good fortune to have a bumper crop and to see their income increase. No, once more the eastern farmers will bear that burden, even though they are already in a precarious situation. The government shows but indifference to their condition, it shows complete disregard for their problems and if, from time to time, it brings in an appearance of solution, they are just half measures, temporary piecemeal solutions.
If you look at page 477 of the Canada Year Book, 1963-64, you will see that the Quebec farmers net income has been continuously decreasing since 1959, while that income shows an almost continued increase for the Saskatchewan and Alberta farmers.
Here are some figures bearing out those findings: in Quebec, in 1959, net income was

Supply-Agriculture
$191,848,000; in 1960, $185,686,000; in 1961, $179,073,000; and, in 1962, $179,668,000. They show a steady decrease, except in 1962 when the situation remained almost the same as the previous year. In Saskatchewan, for instance, in 1959, net income was $240,862,000; in 1960, $372,981,000, that is an increase of over $130 million; in 1961, there was a decrease of $137,792,000, and in 1962 the income was three times as high as the previous year, amounting to $503,795,000.
Everybody is aware of last year's harvests; they will keep up this high level.
We are happy that the western farmers enjoy a good income. But we urge the government to give special attention to the eastern farmers who remain in a state of economic and financial stagnation which is a disgrace. The farmers of Quebec as well as of New Brunswick see their situation getting worse and worse because of problems requiring urgent action by the government.
Proper means have to be taken to make agriculture a paying proposition.
To that end, it must be recognized, or at least recalled that the farmers are the basis of our society and its various structures, and that without them, it would become impossible to hold in position those who are at the higher levels.
Neither would our armed forces go very far if the farmers refused to yield their production. Therefore, in order to be logical, we should admit frankly that we owe our very existence to them.
The farmers, besides being the support of each and everyone, are the largest consumers. They are the ones who largely contribute to our trade, transport, industry and every other sector of our economy.
First of all, Mr. Chairman, I would like to list their needs as consumers.
They must have a decent home, as every other citizen does, a heating system and all sorts of equipment and furniture as we all do.
Moreover, the farmer must have huge buildings for his farm, and all the required equipment connected with it.
Farmers need various structures, according to their production.
Moreover, our farmers need various other things, like farm implements and machinery, separators, milking machines, milk coolers, and water pipes, all things which are very expensive.
In addition, they must have a wide range of mechanical equipment, such as tractors, trucks, sowers, fertilizer spreaders, harvesters or combines, hay presses, threshing and binding machines, and many other items which it would take too long to list.
[Mr. Latullppe.l
They must have a great many other things like chain saws, wood-cutting and working equipment, repair workshops, because they cannot constantly go to the garage or call upon the services of mechanics.
I think that my list is long enough to prove that the farmers are great producers, but also great consumers, and rank first in our economic structure.
Of course, the farmer has to incur many expenses, and it is inconceivable that the government may think that in Quebec, for instance, with an average income lower than $1,500, he can manage to meet his responsibilities. It is a mathematical as well as an economic impossibility, which has consequences in other fields.
The farmer, whoever he may be, needs machines and tools. The government should without delay study means to allow grants to farmers, in order to help them pay for the machinery without which, today, it is impossible to farm on a profitable basis.
Likewise, grants should be allowed for fertilizers, in order to help the farmer increase his production potential and improve the quality of his products.
Indeed, money can be found to make war machinery, machinery designed to destroy. I believe the government and the Canadians are clever enough to make production machinery intended to assist agriculture and maintain life in a country where citizens wish only to live.
Our economists and our ministers of finance often speak of economic cycles. By way of simplification of great theories, I may say it is undeniable that when agriculture is prosperous at home, all other sectors of our economic life benefit.
We all know that farmers can produce. I have given proof that they are also great consumers. The basic law of economy, the law of supply and demand, proves that by improving the lot of farmers, we would give our economy a shot in the arm which is badly needed at the present time.
Mr. Chairman, it is unthinkable and intolerable that the government does not give greater attention to agriculture. Instead of a reduction in the budget in relation to the balance of expenses, a tremendous increase in the estimates of this department would have been necessary to face the alarming situation which prevails now.
Previous governments always thought that the farm credit board, through farm loans, would save farmers from their precarious financial situation. On the contrary, in the majority of cases, this board served only to put farmers into debt, and the loans that

were made helped only in crippling farmers who did not have the means to repay the loan.
Our farmers, who have long operated on a submarginal basis, had to obtain loans, to go into debt. However, their products have consistently sold at a price lower than the current price. The farmer does not want all kinds of loans, new financing systems, but rather to be able to sell his products at a reasonable profit, in order to meet his obligations.
In my opinion, the best way to help farmers would be to set up market prices that would enable farmers to sell their products at a profit, because more than 80 per cent of farmers in the province of Quebec operate on a submarginal basis. In the circumstances, how is it possible to be prosperous in a province or in a country? So it is the responsibility of the Minister of Agriculture to take under consideration the suggestions I am making.
Since the farmer does not have the required income to pay his debts, he cannot make the necessary improvements to modernize his operations, so that his expansion will keep pace with industrial and technical developments, and be competitive with any commercial product that can be put on the market.
A farmer should be exempted from that shameful 11 per cent tax because he is one of the largest consumers of building materials of all kinds since he is always building something. He needs all types of constructions. Why should he pay that 11 per cent tax?
What happens is that the farmer can no longer hope to compete on an equal footing with other areas of the economy. People are leaving the farm to live in the city, thus adding to the number of unemployed. There is nothing in farming to encourage young people to try and make a future of it. We cannot blame the young generation for showing little interest in agriculture because it is not a paying proposition.
In some counties over 50 per cent of our farms have been abandoned. The farmers are not the first ones who should be blamed; but rather, the government should be blamed for its inaction and its lack of interest because it is mainly responsible for the present predicament in which farmers find themselves.
I know that the government does not want to do much to organize or increase farm production because there are already surpluses and governments are afraid of them. In a civilized country, it would be logic to be practical and we should recognize that surpluses are not a misfortune for the people, but rather a windfall. The officials of the department are clever enough to find new markets for such surpluses. Why not organize farming on an economic basis?
Supply-Agriculture
I know there are surpluses, but that should be a blessing for the whole population instead of a penalty as our economists try to point out at the present time. Farmers have to pay heavy interest on loans made to them by the farm credit board, that is 5 per cent although the provincial government reimburses 2j per cent. Now, if there is an authority in the field of agriculture, why force a government to take funds out of the general revenue of a province or of the country to pay interest to lending institutions?
The Liberal party has enough clever men to ask those vested interests to make sacrifices and lend that money at a rate of 3 per cent to prevent a province from levying taxes on the tax revenue from all taxpayers.
Everyone must take his responsibilities and I am asking you, hon. members of the government, to take yours and to ask high finance in Canada to take its responsibilities also.
Farmers living on average farms have to pay, out of a meagre income, municipal and school taxes which are getting higher and higher. In my riding, the owner of an average farm pays more than $500 for school and municipal taxes. That is preposterous. Farmers are in a frightful economic situation. You should see them and realize their position before it is too late.
I have here a letter, or rather a request, that people from my riding and from the neighbouring constituencies have sent me. It says:
Hon. Harry Hays,
Minister of Agriculture,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Hays:
Enclosed you will find a petition, signed by a group of farmers in the counties of Compton, Stanstead and Sherbrooke, asking that subsidies now being granted for the transportation of grain by railways also apply in the case of transportation by trucks.
I feel their request is legitimate and that granting it would help substantially to raise the income of farmers in eastern Canada and especially in Quebec.
I hope therefore, Sir, that you will give serious consideration to this letter and that you will be kind enough to set forth the views of both the government and your department on the matter.
Yours truly
I think the hon. gentleman could surely do something about that, because eastern farmers have to import 60 per cent of the feed grain they need. For those reasons, I feel it would be appropriate to subsidize transportation by trucks and that this would be of great assistance to the farmers.

Supply-Agriculture
I also take it upon myself to make a suggestion to the government and especially to the Minister of Agriculture. We know that, during the seeding season, farmers lack farm help while a great many unemployed in our cities do not know what to do and have to be content with unemployment benefits.
Consequently, farmers are wondering whether it would not be possible to extend the winter work period in order that they may hire the help they need, that is unemployed people, to do the bulk of the work. Would it not be possible for the government to pass a special bill in favour of farmers, perhaps under the winter works program, so that salaries could be paid to city people going out to help the farmers?

Mr. Chairman, we have been dealing with the subject of agriculture, particularly the administration item, for some time and I want to conclude on behalf of Her Majesty's loyal opposition by saying that we are very happy that the minister was able to spend two days with us between his peripatetic pilgrimages. While he did not cover the entire field, as one can understand, he did answer a variety of questions that were asked. Therefore may I say on behalf of those for whom I speak that under all the circumstances we feel that this item might now be passed.
There is one matter on which I should have liked to hear him but I do not want to hold up his estimates. That matter is one to which he made reference in the course of his remarks last evening. He said, as I understood him, that he is now in charge of railway branch line rationalization. There is a great deal of interest in this matter, particularly on the prairies, and a general statement by him at a very early date is most necessary and would be most acceptable. Certainly so far as the people of western Canada are concerned they feel strongly that the plans for railway abandonment should be proceeded with very slowly and that rather than piecemeal abandonment there should be railway line consolidation. I do not intend to deal with that at any length, except that I should like to hear the views of the Minister of Agriculture because this is a tremendous field of responsibility which he has assumed.
The right hon. gentleman does not seem to realize that this responsibility has not yet been stripped from me but will be shortly.

As usual the Minister of Transport has interrupted. With a provincial election about to take place in the province of Saskatchewan I have read and heard that he is about to make a visitation there to place
[Mr. Latulippe.l
before the people the true facts in connection with this matter. I would not let him do that. I say to the Minister of Agriculture: You look after your own department and do not let them bite off anything more; do not let them interfere with you. I read the other day that the Minister of Agriculture had said that some of the eastern ministers were very difficult to deal with, and they were exerting pressure on him because they thought he was doing too much for western Canada. All I can say is that anything that can be done to assist agriculture in all sections of the country will receive the support of the opposition at all times. He stated a moment ago that his purpose is to maintain those things that are good, and to make improvements in order to assure an ever-increasing opportunity for farmers, as indeed for all sectors of the community, and in those aims he will receive the fullest support of the opposition.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I am afraid I cannot agree with the right hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. I believe this is about the third or possibly the fourth time he has spoken on these estimates and there are certain hon. members who have not yet had a chance to speak.
I do not mind.

He gave his vinegar speech yesterday and his honey speech today, and if another occasion arises we may have some other variety of speech from him. I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture a problem that is hanging over the heads of some of the farmers in my constituency and which has arisen for two or three reasons. One has to do with the unusually heavy snowfall this winter, together with the fact that the snow is still there. This is very unusual. We have not had a single thaw so far and the result is that as one drives along the highway it is not unusual to see snowbanks 12, 14 or 16 feet high.
Hon. members may recall that some four years ago there were very serious floods in that area. There was a lot of publicity at the time in the national newspapers and on television and a great amount of attention was paid to the situation. Funds were raised to assist the flood victims and the people of the area responded very generously. I believe they raised in excess of $50,000 locally which amount was met by funds from various government departments.
However, at that time one particular group was completely ignored. I refer to the farmers of Mount Joy township. The funds that were raised were all directed toward the assistance of householders who had suffered extensive damage to their homes, furniture

and property. The result was that in the allocation of the funds a farmer could only receive assistance if his home had been damaged. It is well known that farmers show a little more foresight than city dwellers and erect their homes on the highest part of their land. The result was that the farm had to be totally inundated before the farmer's home would be damaged.
Extensive damage was done to the farms. Many of them were strewn with logs, stumps and other debris and there was considerable expense involved in clearing the debris off the land. In addition, the fields were waterlogged, which in many cases resulted in total crop failures. However in spite of this damage these farmers were unable to qualify for the assistance that was provided to the flood victims.
I believe I can understand the reason for that, Mr. Chairman. I do not think that the Department of Agriculture had made any preparations beforehand to meet such a situation, one which could well arise again from time to time in various regions of the country. What I should like to know today is whether the minister or the department has any plans to meet such an emergency, should it be repeated. There is a distinct danger of such a situation arising again in the same area this year because of the unusual circumstances I have outlined. Many of the farmers have not been able to recoup the losses they suffered four years ago and if such a situation should recur many of these farmers, who have had a rather tough time over the last three or four years, in all likelihood would be wiped out. May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO CHANGE RULE RESPECTING INSANITY
AMENDMENT TO CHANGE RULE RESPECTING INSANITY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-14, to amend the Criminal Code (insanity).
He said: I had not expected I would have an opportunity of introducing this bill during this week. I think perhaps it is a very appropriate week in which to introduce a bill dealing with the subject of insanity. The purpose of the bill which I am introducing is to amend the Criminal Code so as to abolish what is known as the M'Naghten rules in respect to criminal insanity and substitute an up to date modern rule in its place.
One man is responsible for this bill being presented before the house. He is a young man by the name of Ronald Markle, who is a constituent of mine, now serving a sentence at Kingston penitentiary. He is 33 years of age, married, with seven children.
Markle suffered from a strange malady. In the course of two or three years he set fire to schools, churches and apartment houses. He was undetected by the police, and there was no rational purpose in his actions. Some time in 1962 he gave himself up to the police and asked for treatment. He pleaded guilty to nine charges of arson in a magistrate's court. He was not represented by counsel, and was convicted and sentenced to a total of 24 years in the penitentiary.
On appeal, the court of appeal saw nothing wrong with this sentence. However the public were more sensitive and a committee of citizens was formed to aid Markle. The press became interested and eventually the former minister of justice, the Hon. Mr. Fleming, directed a new hearing, and on this new hearing the sentence was reduced to 12 years.
Under the laws of Canada in regard to criminal insanity as they presently stand, there is no doubt that Markle was not insane. He appreciated the nature and quality of his actions; he knew that they were wrong. Indeed that was the very reason he gave himself up to the police and asked for treatment. He was, therefore, under our law criminally responsible for his actions. But it is equally clear that his acts were irrational and were the product of mental illness. What Markle needed, and needs, was not punishment but treatment.
The purpose of the bill before the house is designed to amend the inadequate provisions of the Criminal Code in regard to criminal insanity, and bring them up to date and in line with enlightened, modern medical opinion. The purpose of the bill is to ensure that where acts are committed by reason of
Criminal Code
mental illness, the persons involved are considered as sick persons requiring treatment, and not as criminals requiring punishment.
To use the language of a famous American judge, Judge Jerome Frank:
A society that punishes the sick is not wholly civilized; a society that does not restrain the dangerous madman, lacks common sense.
The present bill is designed to abolish the M'Naghten rule of criminal insanity and substitute for it a modern test adopted by the United States court of appeals in 1954.
The M'Naghten rule was framed by English judges in 1843, more than 120 years ago. M'Naghten fatally shot Edward Drummond, secretary to the prime minister, Sir Robert Peel, in an attempt to kill the latter. M'Naghten explained that he had made a mistake; that he desired to kill the prime minister. He gave this further explanation:
The Tories in my native city have compelled me to do this; they follow and persecute me wherever I go and have entirely destroyed my peace of mind.
There is no doubt that M'Naghten suffered from insane delusions. Nine physicians and surgeons called to the witness stand testified that he was insane, and the presiding lord chief justice directed a verdict of not guilty. M'Naghten spent the rest of his life in a mental institution.
The public, however, were indignant at the crime, ascribing it to a political plot. The House of Lords put questions to the 15 English judges who laid down what has since been known as the M'Naghten rules. The basic rule is that to establish a defence on the ground of insanity, it must be proved that the accused was labouring under such a defect of reason from disease of the mind as not to know the nature and quality of the act he was doing or, if he did know it, that he did not know that what he was doing was wrong. This test, slightly altered, remains the law of Canada today. It is contained in section 16 of the Criminal Code, part of which is sought to be repealed by the bill before the house.
The Criminal Code provides that no person shall be convicted of a criminal offence in respect of an act or omission on his part while he was insane, and it goes on to define insanity as follows, in subsection 2:
For the purposes of this section, a person is insane when he is in a state of natural imbecility or has disease of the mind to an extent that renders him incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of an act or omission, or of knowing that an act or omission is wrong.
Subsection 3, which I need not read, goes on to deal with specific delusions. It will be noted that the key phrase is the word "appreciated" and this is used rather than the word "know" in the original M'Naghten

Criminal Code
rules, but since 1843 a very great deal has been learned in the fields of medical and psychiatric knowledge.
In the Durham case in the United States in 1954, an American court of appeals in Washington, D.C., substituted a new rule, which is the basis of the amendment I propose. The provision which that court adopted was that the accused is not criminally responsible if his act was the product of mental disease or mental defect.
Judge Bazelon, who wrote the judgment of the American court of appeals, has made the following statement:
In this century the chorus of protest (against M'Naghten's rules) has become deafening. In a poll taken a few years ago 80 per cent of 300 American psychiatrists pronounced those rules unsatisfactory.
One of the greatest of American judges, Mr. Justice Cardozo stated flatly:
Everyone concedes that the present definition of insanity has little relation to the truths of mental life.
Judge Bazelon tells us that the main criticisms of the right-wrong test are fourfold:
First, it misses the point entirely because whatever ''insanity" means, the term refers to abnormal conditions of mind that cannot all be gathered together under the rubrics, "know" and "wrong." Second, the test is based on an outmoded theory of faculty psychology derived from phrenology.
-a rather ancient science-
-that dividend the topography of the mind into separate compartments. Modern psychology views a man as an integrated personality and reason is only one element of that personality, and not the sole determinant of conduct. Third, the test poses to the expert an ultimate question involving legal and moral, as well as medical issues. Fourth, the test has so strait-jacketed psychiatric testimony that insanity is defined exclusively in terms of extreme psychosis and patent organic deterioration.
From the judicial point of view, Judge Bazelon says:
What all this controversy adds up to, practically, is whether we are to have more and freer psychiatric testimony. I myself have no hesitance in taking the position solidly in favour of freer and fuller expert testimony.
He goes on to state:
This is exactly what we did in the District of Columbia five years ago when the United States court of appeals adopted the Durham rule. Under this new, more liberal rule-
-which description I hope will commend it to the hon. members opposite-
-a modem and comprehensive body of law governing the administration of the insanity defence is being slowly built up on the basis of continuing experience. At the same time, the community's fears that great numbers of dangerous persons would be freed to attack again, are being put to rest. Nothing of this sort has happened. Defendants acquitted under the Durham rule have been sent to mental hospitals, many of them
[Mr. Brewin.l
for longer periods than they would have sewed in prison, and they appear to get into less trouble after release, than prison convicts.
Therefore the fear that is sometimes expressed that if this rule is changed people will be let out and will more readily commit other crimes has no basis in fact.
In 1955 the American law institute, composed of a leading body of distinguished lawyers, judges and scholars, urged the liberalization of the M'Naghten rules. In a recent study sponsored by the American bar foundation in 1962 under the title "The Mentally Disabled and the Law", the following conclusions are reached:
It is desirable to broaden the class of the mentally disabled who are held criminally irresponsible without removing the issue from the jury. The M'Naghten and irresistible impulse tests defined too narrowly the class of persons who should be hospitalized rather than imprisoned. These tests also prevent psychiatric witnesses from presenting an adequate word picture of the defendant's mental condition because they are phrased in terms having little relevance to current learning in the field of psychology. The product test remedies both of these defects.
I am aware, along with other hon. members who are familiar with this subject, that this matter was dealt with in 1957 when a royal commission presided over by Chief Justice McRuer made recommendations contrary to those of the bill I am now placing before the house. It so happens that Chief Justice McRuer was a former partner of mine and of the hon. member for High Park (Mr. Cameron). I worked closely with him as junior counsel and I have the greatest respect for Chief Justice McRuer, a respect which was deepened by my personal knowledge and experience. I know he is held in great respect by members of the legal profession. Nevertheless, I find the dissenting report of that commission, prepared by Her Honour Judge Kinnear and Dr. Jones, professor of psychiatry at Dalhousie University, far more persuasive and compelling. Indeed, with great respect, it seems to me that the chief justice in this report has erred by adopting a too legalistic approach to the problem. He rejected the proposal to amend the Criminal Code upon the basis of the contention that the word "appreciate" in the code substantially differentiates the Canadian law from M'Naghten's rules.
This is a refinement which, as the dissenting report indicates, not even judges and lawyers are able to appreciate.
The preferable view seems to me to be that adopted by the so-called Gowers commission in Britain, which quotes statements of doctors with experience in mental diseases appearing before it, as follows:
The M'Naghten test is based on an entirely obsolete and misleading conception of insanity, since

Insanity does not only or primarily affect the cognitive or intellectual faculties, but affects the whole personality of the patient, including both the will and the emotions.
One or two misconceptions should be cleared up. This change in the law is not proposed because of any softness of outlook toward those who commit criminal offences. Indeed there are many cases in which persons who are mentally ill, but criminally responsible under the M'Naghten rule, receive sentences, serve their terms in jails or penitentiaries and are released while still suffering from mental illness. These people time and again commit further serious crimes.
The real question, after all the theoretical discussion, is whether the proper remedy is punishment or treatment. I know that many people, feeling indignant at the horrible antisocial acts which are sometimes committed, believe the answer is punishment. Unfortunately, punishment works no cure and indeed may intensify the criminal impulses of the person punished. An inmate of a mental hospital, however, should not be released from the hospital until it is certified that he is cured or at least not dangerous to himself or others. Psychiatrists can make mistakes but there is no reason why the law should not direct attention to the right question, which is: Has the person involved been cured of the mental defects which, if he is released, will make him a danger to society? The prison warden at the expiration of a criminal sentence has no right to ask such a question before he lets the prisoner out, possibly to endanger the public.
In the Durham case, the court said:
The legal and moral traditions of the western world require that those who of their own free will and with evil intent commit acts which violate the law, shall be criminally responsible for those acts. Our traditions also require that where such acts stem from and are the product of mental disease or defect, moral blame shall not attach and hence there will not be criminal responsibility.
In our society the essential aim of the criminal law should not be to induce mass fear of punishment but to reaffirm the value of each individual by due process in his conviction and purposeful treatment thereafter.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that this bill which I have introduced will probably suffer the fate of many other private members' bills. It is however my earnest hope that the government will give serious consideration to this matter which I have brought forward.
There are many other fields in which we reject the impact of modern thought and science, but is there any reason why we should insist in our criminal law in asking a question framed 120 years ago, when
Criminal Code
psychiatric knowledge was in its infancy? Is there any reason why this parliament in 1964 should not gain a reputation throughout the civilized world for a modern and enlightened attitude to the question of criminal responsibility? I urge the government to give the most careful attention to the amendment of the criminal law in this respect.
I would like to conclude by quoting the words of Winston Churchill, who in the midst of the darkest days of the world war made the following statement:
The mood and temper of the public with regard to the treatment of crime and criminals is one of the most unfailing tests of the civilization of any country. A calm, dispassionate recognition of the rights of the accused, and even of
the convicted criminal against the state_ Those
are the symbols which, in the treatment of crime and criminals, make and measure the stored-up strength of a nation and are sign and proof of the living virtue in it.
Mr. Speaker, the maintenance of an obsolete and antiquated law of criminal responsibility would show that we in this house in Canada were failing in this test. I suggest it is in this spirit that the members of this house should consider that the time has come to make sure that there are no more cases in Canada like the case of Ronald Markle, now being punished for a crime for which according to our modern knowledge and judgment he was not responsible mentally or morally. If we in this parliament do something about this type of problem we will be measuring up, in Mr. Churchill's words, to one of the "tests of civilization".

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO CHANGE RULE RESPECTING INSANITY
speechtext:
I am
sure the house is grateful to the honourable and learned member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) for bringing to our attention this most important aspect of the criminal law. I trust that if I indicate some difference of opinion between myself and the author of Bill C-14 he would not think I am treating his enlightened efforts in too summary a fashion.
It is true, as the hon. member stated, that we are still administering the law as it was laid down and applied in the trial of Daniel M'Naghten almost a century and a quarter ago. The main criticism of section 16 of our criminal law is, as I understand it, that the law has not kept pace with medical science and knowledge. It is contended that as medical science threw back the frontiers the law has not been modified. That, of course, is the object of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Greenwood.
I am sure the hon. member would agree that his proposition is not a novel one. I do not say that in any desire to detract from the worthiness of his efforts. My purpose and

Criminal Code
my justification are simple. It is my submission that the M'Naghten rules have stood the test of time. While it is true that on one hand the M'Naghten rules have their strong critics, on the other hand there may be found their strong supporters.
I propose, with deliberate economy of language, to outline the historical background of the M'Naghten rules and their progress. Forty years ago-in 1924, to be precise-Lord Justice Atkin headed a 27-man committee, a committee of eminent and outstanding men both in the law and in medicine, who were reinforced by an opinion from the British medical association. They brought forth a recommendation that the M'Naghten rules should be modified. That recommendation died on second reading in the British parliament. In 1953 a royal commission was again established in Great Britain and the question was given searching and careful inquiry. Once more the British medical association came forward, and the committee, armed with their report, went a step further than the Atkin committee and recommended to parliament that the M'Naghten rules be abrogated. Once more that recommendation died in the British House of Commons.
The hon. and learned member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) has stated that in 1957 Chief Justice McRuer headed a commission to examine the same question. I share the hon. member's respect for the chief justice of Ontario and I should like to put on the record the conclusions of the majority report, which may be found at page 46 of the report and which reads in part as follows:
There should he no change in subsection 1, 2 and 4 of section 16 of the Criminal Code.
Then the majority report goes on to deal with the law suggested by the hon. member for Greenwood, sometimes known as the laws of the state of New Hampshire. This is what the report said:
The repeal of section 16 and the substitution of the laws of the state of New Hampshire or those of the district of Columbia would not make for a better administration of justice in Canada.
How is it that the M'Naghten rules, subjected to the severest criticism, have withstood the onslaughts of medical associations, of legal committees and royal commissions? An appropriate consideration in answering that question, I suggest, is to determine the purpose for which the M'Naghten rules were formulated. The object of the criminal law, as I understand it, is to protect society, and while there should be other considerations than deterrence, nonetheless the prime purpose of the law is to protect society from the depredations of dangerous and vicious people.

It should be borne in mind that the M'Naghten rules are not set forth as an all-embracing definition of insanity. Perhaps it is more accurate to say that they do not define insanity at all. They set forth a standard of criminal responsibility.
In that regard I wish to point out-and I cannot emphasize this too strongly-that even in 1843 when the judges brought forth the M'Naghten rules, they were aware of the fact that the medical association had a much broader view as to the definition of insanity. But the judges who brought forth the M'Naghten rules started from the fundamental proposition that every person is presumed to be sane and responsible in law for his acts. Then they went a step further and said that if the person desired to escape criminal responsibility it must be proved that either he did not know the nature and quality of his act, or if he did know it, he did not know that it was wrong. The hon. and learned member for Greenwood pointed out in his lucid statement that this is putting the question in the strait-jacket of the right or wrong test. He calls to our attention that modern medical science shows that you cannot, in determining insanity, put the human mind into separate compartments and determine this question solely on the principles of reason, and it must be determined by looking at the whole human function. I concede that, judged solely by medical standards, it is difficult to defend the M'Naghten rules, but I respectfully suggest that in practice they have worked and I am not aware of any substantial miscarriage of justice because they have been maintained in the Criminal Code.
I would, in this great conflict between the M'Naghten rules and the medical association, borrow the words of Mr. John Robinette, the treasurer of the Law Society of Upper Canada and one of the leaders of the bar in this country. This is what he said in giving his opinion before the royal commission:
It seems to me that it might be worthy of consideration to exclude from the code entirely the word insanity, and what is now section 16 should merely provide that under certain circumstances a person shall not be criminally responsible for his acts or omissions, leaving out any reference to insanity because I think that is probably what causes some of the controversy between the medical profession and the legal profession.
There is a general maxim that if the law satisfies the public conscience, then it is doing its duty. It is my humble and respectful submission that over the years the M'Naghten rules have satisfied the conscience of the majority of the people in this country and no one can place his finger on any substantial miscarriage of justice because the rules are still in the Criminal Code. I do not, Mr. MARCH 31, 1964
Speaker, pose as any authority in this matter although I have had occasion to defend people charged with capital murder and have argued this subject matter in the court of appeal with divided success. But I respectfully submit that no matter what it is you put to a jury, whether it be the M'Naghten rules or the watered down and broader rules suggested in Bill No. C-14, invariably the jury will ask themselves this question, "Did the man know that what he was doing was wrong?" In this connection I would bring to the attention of the house that even under Bill No. C-14 psychiatrists would concede that a man, even by their standards, could be insane and would yet know that what he was doing was wrong. I do not propose to weary the house with a long list of legal citations; suffice it to say that several cover my point. In the leading case in Australia, Sodeman v. The King, the defence were able to bring forth three medical experts who all testified, without reservation, that the accused man did not know the nature and quality of his act and did not know that it was wrong. The prosecution brought forth no evidence in rebuttal. The jury convicted, and subsequent appeals failed.
I have had occasion to make a study of five cases reported in the British Notable Trials series, all involving a defence on the grounds of insanity. On each occasion medical evidence was brought forth to show that the accused man did not know the nature and quality of his act, and on each occasion a verdict of guilty was recorded. That brings me back to my original proposition, that while in theory the M'Naghten rules are open to great criticism, in practice they have worked and any other rule that might be substituted would also be subjected by the jury to the searching question, "Did the man know it was wrong when he committed the act?"

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question? Does he think that because a man like Markle knew that what he was doing was wrong, but nevertheless acted as a result of mental illness, it is appropriate that he should be treated as a criminal and should not receive treatment as a sane person?
